candidates.headline: 24-Hour Economy targets 30,000 jobs with pharmaceutical park at Ningo Prampram …Today is deadline for drugmakers to register interest
candidates.evidence: The government has opened registration for pharmaceutical manufacturers to establish operations in the Legon Pharmaceutical Innovation Park (LePIP), a 2,000-acre facility planned at Ningo Prampram in the Greater Accra Region. The project, being developed by the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development (24H+) Authority with the Ghana Infrastructure and Investment Fund (GIIF), is expected to create wealth and an estimated 30,000 jobs, according to the Authority. Companies have until today (October 12) to submit expressions of interest. About 70 per cent of Ghana’s pharmaceutical demand is met through imports, costing the country more than $300 million annually, the call for expressions of interest says. The government has set a target of replacing 50 per cent of imports with locally produced medicines by 2030. The Authority describes LePIP as Ghana’s first integrated pharmaceutical innovation park, designed to make the country a manufacturing and export hub for West Africa and beyond. Under the plan, a special purpose vehicle will provide shared infrastructure, including power, water and steam meeting Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, an effluent treatment plant, cold-chain warehousing and ready-built factory shells. The Authority stresses that the exercise is not a tender and confers no lease, award or equity right. Shortlisted firms will be invited to bilateral discussions from October 26 this year. The UK-funded Ghana Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) Programme is supporting the process.

candidates.headline: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
candidates.evidence: Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore. Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists. The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles. Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said. “It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.” There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many. With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance. Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory.

candidates.headline: Bangladesh seeks removal of Indian export barriers, anti-dumping duties - Sarabangla English
candidates.evidence: Bangladesh has urged India to remove restrictions on Bangladeshi exports, including land port-related barriers and non-tariff obstacles, and withdraw anti-dumping duties imposed on Bangladeshi products. The issues were raised at the 16th meeting of the Bangladesh-India Joint Working Group on Trade, held in New Delhi on October 8–9. The two-day meeting focused on easing bilateral trade barriers, improving land port facilities and strengthening regional connectivity. Bangladesh called for a review of restrictions affecting the entry of its goods into the Indian market, as well as the removal of anti-dumping duties on jute products and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) film. It also sought continued tariff preferences for Bangladeshi exports to India after the country graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category. The Bangladeshi delegation emphasised improving market access, harmonising product standards and simplifying certification procedures, including requirements under the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). Dhaka also proposed expanding the movement of goods to Nepal and Bhutan through Indian territory to facilitate regional trade. candidates.headline: ACLU Statement on President Trump’s Latest Attack on the International Criminal Court | American Civil Liberties Union
candidates.evidence: NEW YORK - Today, the Trump administration announced sanctions on the entire International Criminal Court, only hours after one of the court’s former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize. Previously, the United States had sanctioned specific ICC officials, a UN human rights expert, and three Palestinian human rights groups. The international community, including the United States, established the ICC in 1998 to help maintain international peace and security. The ICC investigates and prosecutes atrocity crimes when domestic legal systems are unwilling or unable to do so. 125 countries have joined the international treaty creating the ICC, known as the “Rome Statute.” While the United States has not ratified the Rome Statute, it has supported the ICC’s critical work on a wide range of matters under both Democratic and Republican administrations. “The Trump administration's continued attempts to dismantle the International Criminal Court are disastrous for global justice and human rights accountability,” said Jamil Dakwar, director of the ACLU's Human Rights Program.

candidates.headline: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
candidates.evidence: BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. candidates.headline: Largest 2D map of the universe helps scientists discover new gravitational lenses - Science Tech Updates
candidates.evidence: Using data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, with help from artificial intelligence, an international team of scientists has discovered 70 new gravitational lenses—rare cosmic alignments that act as natural magnifying glasses. The new lenses further expand one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date and will allow scientists to study dark matter, galaxy evolution and the structure of the universe. In August 2026, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team released the largest 2D map of the universe ever created. The 5.6-trillion-pixel map contains nearly 4 billion celestial objects, including stars, galaxies, black holes and asteroids. This map was created using data from three ground-based sky surveys: The Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS) was conducted using the 570-megapixel Department of Energy (DOE)–fabricated Dark Energy Camera (DECam), mounted on the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at NSF Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile, a program of NSF NOIRLab. In an extensive follow-up study published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, led by Emerald Lin (an undergraduate student at UC Berkeley) and Ivonne Toro Bertolla (a research assistant at NSF NOIRLab and science operations assistant at Las Campanas Observatory), the team spectroscopically confirmed 70 of the candidates, establishing them as true instances of gravitational lensing. These natural telescopes allow astronomers to study objects that would otherwise be too distant or faint to detect. They can magnify galaxies from the early universe, reveal the presence and distribution of invisible dark matter, help improve measurements of the universe’s expansion rate and enable the detection of exoplanets—planets orbiting other stars. AI narrows the search “The DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys’ deep and wide-field images have provided an unprecedented foundation for discovering new gravitational lenses,” says Aleksandar Cikota, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab, co-author of the study and PI of the follow-up observing program. “Each confirmed lens adds to a resource that will benefit the entire astronomical community,” says Cikota. “Together, we are building a powerful foundation for future discoveries.” https://noirlab.edu/public/blog/desi-legacy-imaging-surveys/ Scitechupdates.com is a participant in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program, other affiliate and advertising programs, designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees to support the running of this educational site.

candidates.headline: Intensive breathwork reduces brain blood flow and alters neural communication
candidates.evidence: Intensive breathing exercises can reduce blood flow to the brain by up to 45% and alter communication between brain networks, according to a new brain-imaging study. Participants reported experiences resembling some effects of psychedelic drugs, including altered perception, vivid mental imagery, a sense of unity and changes in self-experience. The researchers, presenting the work at the ECNP Congress in Munich, say changes in brain communication, rather than reduced blood flow alone, appear to be key to the altered state. The study involved 30 healthy, experienced breathwork practitioners who performed high-ventilation breathwork during MRI scanning. Participants reported strong altered states of consciousness, describing a predominantly oceanic state – in other words, a deep feeling of connection to the universe - resembling that of a moderate to high dose of LSD or psilocybin, albeit with less pronounced visual effects. Brain imaging showed that global grey-matter cerebral blood flow fell by around 45% during the session, on average from 16.24 to 9.81 ml/100g/min. Those who reported stronger altered states also showed greater changes in the brain's default mode network, which is involved in self-reflection and self-related thinking. The researchers suggest that the intensity of the experience is not simply explained by reduced blood flow. Lead researcher Dr Christian Schmitz, Central Institute of Mental Health, Mannheim in Germany, said: " Many people who practice intensive breathwork report profound changes in perception and self-experience, yet the underlying brain mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our study suggests that these experiences are linked not only to marked changes in cerebral blood flow, but also to alterations in how key brain networks communicate". 'Co-Coordinator, Hana Adolphi said, " Breathwork is a legal, inexpensive and non-pharmacological intervention that may provide a valuable tool for studying altered states of consciousness. Understanding these mechanisms could also help inform future research into novel approaches for mental health treatment. Nevertheless, this was a relatively small study, and the findings should be considered preliminary. Larger studies will be needed to determine whether these brain changes have clinical relevance." Commenting, Dr Guy Fincham (Brighton and Sussex Medical School, UK) said: "This study is intriguing as it is starting to extend findings from recent breathwork research that intensive breathing practices may yield altered states of consciousness which individuals describe in ways analogous to psychedelic compounds, and under brain-imaging conditions. These findings are important because such altered subjective experiences may be harnessed for the improvement of mental health, and an accessible non-pharmacological route such a breathwork could prove invaluable for many. We should note that the study was uncontrolled and the sample was made up of experienced practitioners, so replication of this in breathwork-naïve participants using a randomised-controlled design will help determine whether these findings can translate more widely and produce therapeutic benefit".
